judgements.reason: Drug addiction, illegal narcotics, municipal public-health policy, and medically supervised treatment were intelligible by 1930; narcotics-maintenance clinics had even existed in the United States in the early 1920s. The modern-sounding label “safe havens” does not prevent the policy proposal from being understood.

All the underlying concepts existed by 1930: illegal drugs (opiates and cocaine were criminalized, e.g., the US Harrison Act of 1914), drug addiction as a recognized social and medical problem, and medical supervision of addicts. In fact, narcotic maintenance clinics where addicts received drugs under medical supervision operated in the US and elsewhere in the 1910s–1920s, so the idea of a supervised facility for drug use was intelligible and debatable. The modern term 'safe haven' does not make the concept anachronistic.

The concepts of drug addiction, illegal drugs, and medical supervision were well understood by 1930. Furthermore, the idea of medically supervised drug use was not purely hypothetical, as morphine maintenance clinics for addicts had operated in the United States during the early 1920s before being shut down by the federal government.
